title: Booleans, runes and the difference between byte, rune and character

videos.script: Lesson 7 was about numbers. This one is about two types that do not look like numbers, and one thing that really is not a number at all. {{bool}} First, bool. Go has true and false, and nothing else counts as either. A number in an if statement does not compile, and you will see the message. {{rune}} Then text, one piece at a time. Go has no char type. It has byte and rune, and both of them are integers under another name. A letter in single quotes is a number, and you can do arithmetic with it. {{bytes}} Then the surprise. The letter é is one rune, but a string spends two bytes on it. An emoji takes four. {{chars}} Last, what a reader calls a character. Sometimes that is two runes, and a flag is two runes drawn as one picture. Go's standard library does not split text into those. {{count}} By the end you can give three different lengths for one word, and say which one a question was asking for.
